Baby & Child

Can exercise make you taller? Ten movements and what they really do

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

It is easy to mistake a promise of better posture for a promise of extra height. These ten popular activities can be considered for movement and fitness, but their benefits need to be separated from unsupported claims about growing taller.

Exercise supports your body, but does not lengthen adult bones

Hanging, stretching and swimming are often promoted as ways to gain several centimetres in a short time. Once the growth plates in the long bones have closed, these activities cannot reopen them or make the bones longer. Working harder or following a routine for more months does not overcome that biological limit.

Exercise can still improve strength, movement and how comfortably you hold yourself upright. A change in posture is different from permanent skeletal growth. Set goals around function and enjoyment rather than treating a height measurement as a test of effort or discipline. Being shorter than someone else does not mean you have done something wrong.

Why growth does not stop on the same birthday for everyone

Height reflects inherited traits alongside nutrition, hormones, health and development. Much of the increase happens during childhood and puberty. Growth usually slows as puberty finishes, but its timing varies. Eighteen is not an exact biological cutoff for every person, and being in your twenties does not itself prove that more growth is possible.

A teenager who develops later than peers may still have growth ahead. A clinician can assess the pattern when there is a concern; online exercise claims cannot establish whether growth plates remain open. Neither a particular sport nor a special food guarantees extra height beyond what development allows.

Before trying the ten movements

The following activities are options for mobility or fitness, not a height-increase programme. You do not need to complete all ten, hold every stretch for a minute, or repeat painful movements to make progress. Start gently, move in a controlled way and choose a range that feels comfortable.

If you have an injury, a joint or bone condition, recent surgery, or are pregnant, ask a physiotherapist or another qualified professional which movements suit you. Yoga positions may need modification. Stop an exercise that causes pain, dizziness, tingling or loss of control. A qualified instructor can help with unfamiliar movements.

1. Hanging: optional movement, not a way to add height

A supported hang from a properly installed exercise bar may be part of an individual exercise routine. It is not necessary for getting taller. Avoid jumping at an unstable bar or suspending yourself somewhere that creates a fall risk. If you try it, keep the movement controlled and use foot support where appropriate.

Shoulder comfort, grip and the ability to get down safely matter more than a target hold time. Do not force a straight-arm hang through pain or assume that a thirty-second hold repeated three times is right for everyone. People with shoulder instability or other upper-limb problems should obtain advice before using a hanging exercise.

2. Pelvic lifts: think of a gentle bridge

The movement sometimes called a pelvic shift resembles a bridge. Lie on your back with knees bent and feet resting on the floor. Gently engage the muscles around your trunk and buttocks, then lift the pelvis only as far as you can control comfortably. Lower slowly rather than dropping back down.

Keep the movement through the hips and trunk instead of forcing a large arch in the lower back or putting weight through the neck. The exercise may help with strength and control when appropriate to your needs. It does not stretch the pelvis into a longer skeleton. A physiotherapist can choose suitable repetitions and holds.

3. Side bends: a comfortable reach

Stand in a steady position, with feet about hip-width apart if that helps balance. Slowly bend a little to one side without twisting or jerking, then return to the middle. Repeat on the other side within a comfortable range. You can keep an arm by your side rather than clasping both hands overhead.

Reaching above the head is optional and may be uncomfortable for some shoulders. There is no need to keep the feet tightly together or insist on a fixed twenty-second hold. The purpose is gentle movement along the side of the body, not pulling the spine or leg bones into a permanently longer shape.

4. Puppy pose: make room for an easier version

In yoga, puppy pose starts from hands and knees, then the hands move forward as the chest lowers toward the mat. Keep the hips near the knees and move only as far as your shoulders and back allow. Let the toes rest naturally; there is no need to interlock them or force the chest to the floor.

Keep breathing, avoid straining the neck and come out of the position if it hurts. A teacher can suggest support under the chest or another position when weight through the knees or shoulders is unsuitable. This is a flexibility exercise, not a treatment for short stature, and a full-minute hold is not a requirement.

5. Cobra-style extension: avoid pushing to the maximum

A gentle back extension begins lying on the front, with the hands near the shoulders or the forearms providing support. Raise the chest a small amount only if comfortable, keeping the lower body relaxed. There is no need to straighten the elbows fully, lift the chin sharply or squeeze into the deepest possible bend.

Some people benefit from an individually chosen extension exercise; others need a different movement. Stop if back or leg pain worsens and seek advice rather than increasing the repetitions. Cobra is not a method for lengthening the spine, and five repeated thirty-second holds should not be treated as a universal prescription.

6. Jogging: build endurance gradually

Running can support cardiovascular fitness and, when suitable, provides weight-bearing activity. It does not make adult leg bones longer. For a beginner, alternating walking and easy jogging is often a more practical starting point than trying to run continuously or add distance rapidly.

Use a manageable pace, allow recovery and choose a route and footwear that suit you. Do not run through an injury in pursuit of height. Walking or another comfortable activity can be a useful alternative. In growing children, running belongs within varied, enjoyable activity rather than a promise that exercise will produce a particular adult height.

7. Jumping: fitness benefits do not depend on jumping higher

Skipping and other suitable jumping activities can contribute to bone-strengthening exercise during childhood and adolescence. They do not stretch the legs longer in proportion to the number of jumps. Start with an activity appropriate to age, coordination and joint comfort; a lower-impact option may be preferable for some people.

A home trampoline is not needed for this purpose. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises families to avoid trampolines for children because of injury risk. Turning a height goal into repeated high jumps adds no proven growth benefit. Choose safe play or coached activity for enjoyment and fitness instead.

8. Forward bends with feet apart: soften the knees

For a standing forward bend, use a stable stance and hinge gently through the hips. Keep the knees soft rather than locking them. Reach only as far as feels comfortable and return slowly. Touching the floor is not a pass-or-fail test, and another person should not push you downward.

The stretch may be felt behind the thighs or through the back, depending on the movement. It does not lengthen the bones in the legs. If bending causes pain, balance problems or dizziness, stop and ask about another option. Comfortable movement matters more than copying the depth shown in an exercise photograph.

9. Standing toe reaches: a variation, not an extra growth technique

A second standing stretch with the feet closer together is closely related to the forward bend. It does not offer a separate mechanism for increasing height. Keep enough space between the feet to feel stable and avoid forcing the knees straight or rounding down simply to touch the toes.

You can leave this variation out if you already have a comfortable stretch or if it does not suit your body. There is no benefit in completing duplicate movements solely to finish a ten-exercise checklist. Ask an instructor to help select a position that fits your mobility rather than aiming for someone else’s reach.

10. Swimming: choose a stroke for comfort and skill

Swimming is an aerobic activity that can support fitness and offers a different way to move from running or jumping. Breaststroke is not a proven height-increasing stroke, and stretching the arms and legs through water cannot make closed growth plates active again. Choose strokes you can perform comfortably and safely.

Use appropriate supervision and water-safety practices, and learn technique from a qualified instructor when needed. If a stroke causes shoulder, neck or knee discomfort, adjust the activity rather than pushing through it. For children, swimming is one enjoyable option among many, not a requirement for normal growth.

Build a routine around what improves daily life

A sustainable routine might combine an enjoyable aerobic activity with appropriate strength and mobility work. Look for changes such as easier movement, more comfortable posture, improved endurance or greater confidence in a skill. These are useful outcomes even if the number on the height chart does not change.

Avoid products or programmes that guarantee rapid centimetre gains from stretches. A child should not be pressured into painful exercise or restrictive eating to change their appearance. Consistent opportunities to move, eat adequately and rest are part of supporting health; they are not a contract for a specific height.

When growth concerns deserve a clinical assessment

For children and adolescents, the pattern over time is more informative than a single comparison with classmates. Discuss slowed growth, a change in growth-chart pattern or concerns about puberty with a clinician. Family height and the timing of family members’ puberty may help explain the pattern.

An assessment may include previous measurements, medical history and, when indicated, blood tests or a hand-and-wrist X-ray. Treatment depends on the cause. Growth hormone is a specialist medicine for selected conditions, not a general height supplement. Adults concerned about a new loss of height or persistent back symptoms should also seek individual advice.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

After growth plates close, exercise cannot restart lengthwise bone growth.

Choose movement for fitness and comfort; evaluate a child’s growth pattern clinically when there is concern.

How BeMama can help

Support a positive relationship with movement and body size. Avoid making a child’s height a measure of effort or success.

When to seek help

This is general education, not an individual exercise prescription. Stop painful movements and obtain advice for an injury, relevant condition or growth concern.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Adult height does not increase through stretches or sport once growth plates have closed.
  • All ten activities are discussed as optional movement choices, with gentler technique and realistic expectations.
  • A child’s serial growth pattern and puberty timing matter more than comparison with peers.
  • Hormone treatment requires a specific clinical indication and specialist supervision.

Frequently asked questions

Can exercise make me taller after growth plates close?

No. Stretching, hanging and sport do not lengthen mature bones. They can improve fitness, movement and posture, which are worthwhile goals in their own right.

Does everyone stop growing at eighteen?

No. Puberty and growth-plate closure vary. If a teenager’s growth pattern is concerning, a clinician can assess development rather than relying on a fixed birthday.

Will hanging from a bar permanently lengthen my spine?

It is not a proven way to increase adult height. Do not use painful hangs, added weights or unsafe equipment to chase a promised number of centimetres.

Do I need all ten exercises every day?

No. This is a set of possible movements, not a mandatory routine. Choose appropriate activities and build gradually. Individual advice is useful if you have pain or a health condition.

Should I keep stretching until I touch my toes?

No. Use a comfortable range, keep control and avoid locking the knees or forcing the movement. Reaching the floor says little about the value of an exercise for you.

Is swimming better than running for gaining height?

Neither is a proven way to add height after growth is complete. They provide different fitness benefits; preference, health and access can guide your choice.

Will more jumping make a child grow taller?

There is no reliable extra-height promise. Suitable jumping can be part of varied activity, but repeated high jumps or home-trampoline use are not necessary for healthy growth.

What if one of these movements causes pain?

Stop that movement. Persistent, severe or worsening symptoms need assessment. A physiotherapist or qualified instructor may suggest a different exercise rather than asking you to push harder.

When should I ask about my child’s growth?

Ask if growth seems to slow, the child changes growth-chart pattern or puberty raises concern. Bring previous measurements if available. Being short alone does not automatically mean a disease is present.

Should I buy growth supplements or hormones?

Do not self-prescribe hormones or trust guaranteed height gains. A clinician should investigate a suspected deficiency or growth disorder and explain whether any treatment is appropriate.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
